Let's draw a diagram describing our situation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13934287/assets/eb1176b4a5e2565fceb03e9af652a6ae875f5ee678c103405045fcebc36342e1.png)

First, we find the equation of the line that's perpendicular to $y=-x+2$ and passes through the point $(-1,-3).$

 The given line has a slope of $-1,$ so our perpendicular line must have a slope of $1.$

Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the perpendicular line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y+3 & =1(x+1) \\ y+3 & =x+1 \\ y & =x-2\end{aligned}
$$

We now find the point where the two lines intersect. To do this, we solve the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=-x+2 \\ y=x-2\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this system by putting the two equations equal to one another and solving for $x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-x+2 & =x-2 \\ -x-x & =-2-2 \\ -2x & =-4 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=2$ into either of the two equations gives $y=0.$ So, our solution is $x=2$ and $y=0.$ Therefore, the lines intersect at the point $(2,0).$

Finally, we find the distance $d$ between the points $(-1,-3)$ and $(2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{({x}_{2}-{x}_{1})^{2}+({y}_{2}-{y}_{1})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2-(-1))^{2}+(0-(-3))^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+9} \\  & =\sqrt{18} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the shortest distance between the point $(-1,-3)$ and the line $y=-x+2$ is $3\sqrt{2}.$
